newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Views on copper diverge at Australian conference.
newsitem.headline: Views on copper diverge at Australian conference.

text.p: Differing views on the direction the copper market will take in the aftermath of the Sumitomo Corp trading scandal emerged at an industry conference in Melbourne on Monday.

On one side, John Champagne, former president of Magma Copper Co of the United States and current chief operating officer of New York-based trader Global Minerals and Metals Corp, asserted that most commodities forecasters were wrong in assessing that demand was waning while supplies were increasing.
In particular, China remained a ready buyer of copper on the international market to fuel internal industrial growth and supplement shortfalls in domestic production, Champagne said.
"At the end of the day they have an undeniable need for copper," Champagne told the conference.
He attempted to refute claims by some in the marketplace that China was only a way-station for thousands of tonnes of unwanted copper waiting to be re-exported onto world markets.
Demand for refined copper in China was growing by about 10 percent a year from the current level of over one million tonnes, Champagne said.
Jim Lennon, an analyst for Macquarie Bank of Australia, agreed that China needed to import copper and projected that it would import about 250,000 tonnes of copper this year.

Continuing strength in U.S. demand for copper, notably in the housing and automobile manufacturing sectors, as well as robust markets in Japan and the Republic of South Korea were also helping keep supplies in check, Champagne said.

"There appears to be little real reason for pessimism regarding the outlook for copper and very good reasons to expect that copper will outperform most other non-ferrous and precious metals into the 21st century," Champagne said.
The effect of the Sumitomo scandal on world copper markets was easing over time, he said.
At this point, forward selling by producers coupled with sellers of put options protecting their positions and market speculation were teaming to keep prices under US$1.00 a lb, Champagne said.
Sources said institutional business had largely ranged between US$1,870 and $1,970 a tonne since the Sumitomo scandal, cushioning losses on their put options and delta hedge positions.

However, Chris Torrible, an analyst for commodities forecaster CRU International, told the conference that beyond any short-term recovery in copper prices, "a period of low prices seems almost unavoidable."
Prices plummeted in mid-June after Sumitomo revealed that its former top trader, Yasuo Hamanaka, had racked up trading losses now put at $2.6 billion.
Copper will come under pressure at some point, reflecting high levels of investment in new production, Torrible said.

"On top of new mine projects, close to two million tonnes per year of additional mine production by 2001 could come from expansions, with the largest chunk of this from expansions of greater than 100,000 tonnes per year," Torrible said.
He said any hopes of a bottleneck emerging at the smelting stage to "save the market" was out of the question.
A boom in investment in smelting is ocurring in parallel with that in mining, Torrible said.

"With several new smelters and major expansions planned, western world smelter capacity should rise by about 1.5 million tonnes between the end of 1995 and 2001," he said. --Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
